title: DARK MANSIONS: AI, Innovation, and Fermat’s Last Theorem
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video available here . Yiu, Kosoy, and Gopnik (2024) argue that “Cultural evolution depends on a fine balance between imitation and innovation.” Writing in a world prior to reasoning models, they argued that large language models fall squarely on the imitation side. This paper—focused principally on formal and scientific innovation—proposes a finer-grained, three-tier taxonomy: Tier 1 is transmission, Tier 2 is something new (invention) within a fixed problem formulation, and Tier 3 is framework-generating innovation. Tier 3 requires both historical novelty—a new construction or framework—and functional novelty—a downstream dividend, where the apparatus introduced to solve a problem helps to reorganize later work. We explore Andrew Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem as a case of Tier 3 innovation. Core elements of the proof architecture—especially the R = T modularity-lifting strategy and Taylor–Wiles patching—were not present in the prior mathematical literature. Moreover, the proof apparatus has had substantial downstream impact on number theory and the Langlands program. We consider whether a current frontier AI system trained on pre‑1987 mathematical sources could have produced a Wiles-type proof strategy, and offer reasons for doubt. Broadening the argument beyond the Wiles proof, we analyze three current AI paradigms for AI in mathematics and argue that they do not yet offer clear mechanisms for Tier 3 innovation. We then assess the empirical record of AI-assisted mathematical discovery, including the refutation of the unit-distance conjecture and the proof of the existence of non-sofic groups. We find a growing number of striking Tier 2 achievements, but no evidence yet of Tier 3 innovation. Tier 3 innovation, we propose, depends on three capacities—imagination, judgment, and tenacity, understood functionally as capacities for novel decomposition, structural evaluation, and sustained exploration. Current architectures have not shown these capacities at the scale required for Tier 3 innovation. The paper concludes with reflections on the architectural changes that may be needed for the innovation that comes from what Andrew Wiles vividly describes as stumbling around in “dark mansions.” Bio: Joshua Cohen is a political philosopher. He has written on issues of democratic theory, freedom of expression, religious freedom, political equality, democracy and digital technology, good jobs, and global justice. His books include On Democracy (with Joel Rogers); Democracy and Associations ( with Joel Rogers); Philosophy, Politics, Democracy ; Rousseau: A Free Community of Equals ; and The Arc of the Moral Universe and Other Essays . He is co-editor of the Norton Introduction to Philosophy , now in its third edition. Cohen taught at MIT (1977-2005), Stanford (2005-2014), is currently on the faculty at Apple University, and is Distinguished Senior Fellow in Law, Philosophy, and Political Science at University of California, Berkeley. Cohen held the Romanell-Phi Beta Kappa Professorship in 2002-3; gave the Tanner Lectures at UC Berkeley in 2007; the Comte Lectures at LSE in 2012; and the Annual Lecture on Ethics and AI at Oxford in 2024. He is co-editor-in-chief of Boston Review . Sponsorship of an event does not constitute institutional endorsement of external speakers or views presented. title: Statistically-Grounded Methods for Meaningful LLM Evaluation
content: Video
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video Abstract: In cognitive science, the well-established task of statistical learning, i.e., picking up hidden regularities in sequences, has been linked to neural plasticity in humans. However, we found that LLMs are able to learn a hidden automaton structure entirely in context, simply by feeding them valid sequences from the automaton, and they learn it even faster when the structure reappears with new vocabulary. Building on this, I present Agentic Automata Learning, a framework to formalize what agents can infer from an environment. The agent's task is to identify a hidden automaton by querying an oracle. The framework generates instances of controllable difficulty and tests planning, hypothesis formation and memory, with formal efficiency metrics. We find that frontier models struggle as automata grow, their queries become less informative over time, and they fail at both planning and reasoning from evidence. Providing the agent with stateful scaffolding helps but doesn't close the gap. These results point to inferring structure from interaction as a key open challenge for building agents that can operate in unfamiliar environments. Bio: Gili Lior is a Ph.D. candidate in Natural Language Processing at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, advised by Prof. Gabriel Stanovsky. Her work has dealt with cognitively-motivated analysis and comparison between humans and LLMs, and her current research focuses on human-motivated LLM evaluations, leveraging statistical models to ensure that metrics reflect what users actually care about. She is also a research intern at Google Research working on evaluations of long horizon agentic tasks, and has previously interned at IBM Research and the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2). She is a recipient of the Council for Higher Education's fellowship program for excellent female Ph.D. students in hi-tech fields. Sponsor Event organized by PLI Special Event Seminar Lunch Series

title: Securing LLMs Against Prompt Injection for Agentic Applications
content: Video
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video Abstract : Prompt injection is widely recognized as a major security threat to AI agents, in which external untrusted data (websites, documents, and emails) may contain an injected prompt (“Ignore previous instructions and …”) that arbitrarily manipulates an agent’s operations. The best-defended existing LLMs still suffer from near-100% attack success rates (ASRs) under adaptive prompt-injection attacks. In this talk, I will discuss our latest efforts, SecPO and SecOPD, to fine-tune LLMs with an order-of-magnitude lower ASRs (0% -- 13.3%) against the current strongest prompt-injection attacks. Specifically, we (1) separate the trusted prompt and untrusted data into two input channels; (2) simulate strong adaptively attacked training samples for the model to learn robustness from; and (3) design the loss according to a principle that approximates a (nonexistent) secure-and-powerful LLM. Without a noticeable utility drop, our defended Qwen3.6-27B achieves security that generalizes to realistic agentic tasks with multiple trusted and untrusted messages. We fully open our training set with optimized injections, code for our recipe, and the defended model, which is more robust than industry-scale adversarially-trained GPT-5.5 in agentic tasks. Bio : Sizhe Chen is a Computer Science Ph.D. candidate at UC Berkeley’s Berkeley AI Research (BAIR), working with Prof. David Wagner. He studies real-world AI security problems with general and principled solutions. He developed StruQ, Meta-SecAlign, SecPO, and SecOPD, the most robust open LLMs against adaptive prompt injection attacks. His research has been supported by selective industry fundings, including NVIDIA Fellowship, Meta-BAIR Commons, and Google-BAIR Commons. Previously, he obtained an M.Eng. and a B.Eng. from Shanghai Jiao Tong University. https://sizhe-chen.github.io Sponsor Event organized by PLI Special Event Seminar Lunch Series

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description How do learning systems go from isolated fragments of local experience to integrated knowledge that supports reasoning? Kim will present two projects on learning to reason about distal relationships from experience of local ones, in artificial and neural systems. In the first project, we study how transformers perform transitive inference, a classic relational reasoning task requiring inference about indirectly related items (e.g., if A>B and B>C, then A>C). Comparing in-weights learning (IWL) and in-context learning (ICL), we find markedly different patterns of generalization. IWL models learn a linear embedding, which yields transitive inference along with other behavioral effects seen in humans and animals. ICL models can learn to generalize transitively, but only when the training data or auxiliary tasks require it; otherwise they learn a match-and-copy strategy. We replicate these findings in large language models given novel (in-context) or familiar (in-weights) transitive inference problems. In the second project, in collaboration with Josh Jacobs's group, we study representational updating in human MTL neurons after changes to learned sequences. Replicating earlier work [Momennejad et al., 2017], we find that humans integrate changes to reward structure more easily than changes to sequence structure, and further show that these two kinds of change produce different patterns of remapping. We identify tabular RL models that reproduce these patterns and show that these properties extend to transformers. Together, these findings highlight how learning mechanisms in both brains and models determine whether local experience is integrated into structured knowledge.

title: Designing Robots with Intelligent Disobedience
rawEventDetails: Speaker Reuth Mirsky Affiliation Tufts University Details Event Description Abstract: A prevalent assumption in human-robot teaming is that the artificial teammate should be obedient and compliant. In this talk, I challenge the assumption that autonomous robots should always obey instructions and comply with our expectations. I argue that sometimes, to maximize their potential in the team, robots should employ intelligent disobedience . I will use guide dogs as inspiration to discuss several exciting manifestations of intelligent disobedience in AI and robotics: reasoning about other agents, initiating an interaction, providing proactive guidance, and more. Bio: Reuth Mirsky is an Assistant Professor in the Computer Science department and the Mechanical Engineering department at Tufts University. In her research, she seeks algorithms, behaviours, and frameworks that challenge current assumptions made for human-aware AI agents and robots. Reuth is an active member of the AI and HRI research communities. Some of her recent roles are a Track Chair at AAAI and ICAPS, program chair for the symposium on Technological Advances in Human-Robot Interactions (TAHRI), a guest editor in Frontiers of Artificial Intelligence, JAAMAS, and THRI. She was elected for IJCAI 2025 Early Career Spotlight and AAAI 2025 New Faculty Highlights.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description The reading group will explore the intellectual history of machine learning and artificial intelligence, tracing foundational ideas from early theories of neural computation and the perceptron through symbolic AI, the connectionist revival, deep learning, and contemporary foundation models. Rather than studying these methods only in their modern textbook form, we will return to the original papers, debates, and historical context in which they emerged. Sessions will combine readings of foundational work by researchers such as McCulloch and Pitts, Rosenblatt, Minsky and Papert, Hopfield, Rumelhart, Hinton, and McClelland with occasional watch parties featuring archival documentaries, interviews, and television debates from the early history of AI. The group is intended for participants from across machine learning, cognitive science, neuroscience, linguistics, philosophy, and related fields. No prior background in the history of AI or connectionism is required; the goal is to understand not only how major ideas in machine learning work, but why they emerged, what problems they were intended to solve, and how earlier debates continue to shape AI research today.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description It is often claimed that neural networks construct models of the world (“world models”) and don’t merely exploit heuristics. In this sense, they are said to understand their tasks. But it isn’t always clear what having a world model amounts to, or what should count as evidence for or against. This talk has two parts. First, drawing on joint work with Raphaël Millière, Professor Morrison proposes a minimal notion of a world model: a single, unified representation of a task that preserves its structural relations. He explains how this notion sits within a hierarchy of stronger ones, and argue that many disputes about world models are merely verbal. Second, drawing on joint work with collaborators at Columbia and NYU, he applies this framework to the standard example: Othello-GPT, a transformer trained to predict legal moves in Othello. He argues that the evidence is ambiguous once we adopt the right baselines (networks that plausibly use only heuristics) and the right metrics (which attend to patterns of error and the probabilities assigned to unchosen moves). He then introduces another kind of evidence that favors the heuristic interpretation: how quickly the network learns variants of Othello that extend rather than scramble the board’s geometry. He ends by drawing general lessons for attributing world models to neural networks, and by describing similar approaches for attributing algorithms and probabilistic

title: Trust, Sensing, and Learning for Provable Multi-Robot Performance
rawEventDetails: Speaker Stephanie Gil Affiliation Harvard University Details Event Description Abstract Multi-robot systems are physically embodied networks — they sense, move, and communicate through the physical world. The bar for safe decision-making rises as these systems enter safety-critical, real-world settings where they must perform well under uncertainty. Our work shows that physicality is a resource against the two kinds of uncertainty they face: intentional (or adversarial), where data is manipulated by malicious agents, and natural, where aspects of the environment are simply unknown. Most of this talk concerns intentional uncertainty. Here, one way to exploit physicality is by using communication as a sensor. Because the signals robots exchange are difficult to forge, they carry evidence that can be cross-validated to yield a quantifiable likelihood that an agent's data is trustworthy. This is the foundation of cy-trust, in which stochastic observations of trust model an agent's trustworthiness probabilistically from physical rather than cryptographic evidence. Each neighbor's contribution is then weighted by its trust value. Under this framework, we show that consensus, distributed optimization, and other core coordination tasks admit almost-sure convergence with bounded deviation from their nominal performance, even when malicious agents exceed half of a node's connectivity, past the classical Byzantine bound. We support this finding with both theory and hardware experiments under adversarial attack. Against natural uncertainty, we show that real-time sensing can be folded into rollout-based reinforcement learning, where the same machinery reweights futures rather than neighbors. We apply this idea to routing a fleet of robots to stochastically appearing demand and, with Project CETI, to the first autonomous robotic rendezvous with sperm whales at sea. Finally, we preview some of our future work combining trust with long-horizon sequential decision-making, targeting planning that stays provably resilient when the data informing the plan may itself be corrupted. Biography Stephanie Gil is the John L. Loeb Associate Professor of Engineering and Applied Sciences at Harvard University and an Associate Faculty member of the Kempner Institute. Her research focuses on trust and coordination in multi-robot systems, at the intersection of robotics, communication, and learning. Her contributions have been recognized through the DARPA Young Faculty Award (2024), the Office of Naval Research Young Investigator Award (2021), and the National Science Foundation CAREER Award (2019). She was named a 2020 Sloan Research Fellow for her work at the intersection of robotics and communication. She earned her Ph.D. at CSAIL at MIT, specializing in multi-robot coordination and control, and her B.S. at Cornell University.

title: Princeton AI for Science Evaluation Workshop
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description At this historical juncture, the methods of artificial intelligence (AI) are taking on ever more (and ever more foundational) roles in the routine course of science. AI-based tools are projected to transform every stage of the research pipeline, from literature review and hypothesis generation, to the production of synthetic data and data analysis. Increasingly, with the rise of generative AI, AI tools are also put forward as means of arbitration over the scientific research process itself. Proposed functions for AI as scientific arbiter have included AI based peer review, AI based grant review, AI for predicting the replicability of research findings, and AI for science auditing. Such proposals are being put into practice almost as quickly as they can be described, with little oversight or input from relevant expert communities. The workshop seeks to fill this gap by convening scholars with relevant expertise to weigh in on the prospects of AI in science evaluation and its potential ramifications for the future of science. We believe that this timely conversation must include spokespeople from artificial intelligence—both academic and industry, executives and editors at major journals and publishing houses, working scientists, metascientists, and scholars coming from history, philosophy, and sociology of science. This workshop is co-organized by the Center for Information Technology Policy and Data and Intelligent Systems. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description The reading group will explore the intellectual history of machine learning and artificial intelligence, tracing foundational ideas from early theories of neural computation and the perceptron through symbolic AI, the connectionist revival, deep learning, and contemporary foundation models. Rather than studying these methods only in their modern textbook form, we will return to the original papers, debates, and historical context in which they emerged. Sessions will combine readings of foundational work by researchers such as McCulloch and Pitts, Rosenblatt, Minsky and Papert, Hopfield, Rumelhart, Hinton, and McClelland with occasional watch parties featuring archival documentaries, interviews, and television debates from the early history of AI. The group is intended for participants from across machine learning, cognitive science, neuroscience, linguistics, philosophy, and related fields. No prior background in the history of AI or connectionism is required; the goal is to understand not only how major ideas in machine learning work, but why they emerged, what problems they were intended to solve, and how earlier debates continue to shape AI research today.

title: DDSS Connect & Interdisciplinary Exchange
content: Join us for DDSS’s Connect & Interdisciplinary Exchange series where our DDSS Graduate Fellows present on diverse methodologies and technical approaches. This is a great opportunity to network with others working in quantitive social science. There will be 3 sessions throughout the fall semester. title: CITP Seminar: Noam Kantor
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Talk information: TBA Bio: Noam Kantor is a mathematician and a public interest technologist. Kantor has spent his career using his technical skills to advise efforts to hold technology companies accountable for privacy, civil rights, and competition harms. These efforts have spanned the United States Senate as a TechCongress Fellow, the Mozilla policy team, the Federal Trade Commission's Office of Technology, and now as an AI Lab Policy Fellow at the California Attorney General's Office. He has advised on legal and legislative projects with the potential for multi-billion-dollar impact. In his current role, he is working across high-profile consumer protection investigations and lawsuits. Kantor obtained his doctorate in math from Oxford as a Marshall Scholar.
